title: Pattern syntax
summary: Literals, named variables and shadowing, | and ranges, destructuring structs, enums, nested values, tuples, arrays and slices, ignoring with _, _x and .., match guards, @ bindings, and how patterns work with references: & patterns, ref, and default binding modes.

blocks.md: This lesson is a catalogue. Each section shows one piece of pattern syntax with a runnable example. Keep it open as a reference: the table at the end summarizes all of it.

blocks.title: Literals, | and ranges
blocks.md: A literal matches exactly that value. `|` means **or**. `..=` matches an **inclusive range**; ranges work on integers and `char`, and the compiler checks that the range is not empty. A half-open range `a..b` is allowed in patterns too, as is an open-ended `90..`.

blocks.output:
A B F
vowel consonant digit other
blocks.explain: Arms are tried top to bottom, so `'e'` matches the vowel arm before the consonant range.

blocks.title: Named variables and shadowing
blocks.md: A plain name in a pattern is a **new variable** that matches anything. It does not compare against an existing variable with the same name: it shadows it inside the arm. This surprises many beginners:

blocks.output:
Matched, y = 5
at the end: x = Some(5), y = 10
blocks.explain: The `y` in `Some(y)` is a fresh binding of the inner value. To compare against the outer `y`, use a match guard: `Some(n) if n == y`.

blocks.title: Destructuring structs
blocks.md: A struct pattern lists fields: `Point { x: a, y: b }` binds `a` and `b`. When the variable names equal the field names, use the shorthand `Point { x, y }`. Fields can hold literals or nested patterns, which lets one `match` test some fields and bind others. `..` skips the remaining fields.

blocks.output:
a = 0, b = 7
On the y axis at 7
left edge 2, width 10

blocks.title: Destructuring enums and nested values
blocks.md: Enum patterns follow the shape of the variant: nothing for unit variants, parentheses for tuple variants, braces for struct variants. Patterns nest as deep as the data does:

blocks.output:
Move to x 3, y -1
Text message: hello
Change color to hue 0, saturation 160, value 255
The Quit variant has no data.
3'10" and x = 3

blocks.title: Arrays and slices
blocks.md: *Programming Rust* covers array and slice patterns. An **array** pattern has a fixed length: `[r, g, b]`. A **slice** pattern can match slices of different lengths, so it is refutable: `[]` matches only an empty slice, `[x]` exactly one element, and `..` matches any number in the middle. `rest @ ..` binds the skipped part as a sub-slice.

blocks.output:
rgb 255 128 0
empty
one item: 7
a pair: 1 and 2
4 items from 1 to 4
sum 10

blocks.title: Ignoring values
blocks.md:
- `_` matches anything and **does not bind**. Use it for a whole value, a field, or a parameter you do not need.
- `_name` is a **variable** whose name starts with an underscore. It binds (and so it **moves** the value), but the compiler does not warn if it is unused.
- `..` ignores **all remaining** parts of a tuple, tuple struct or struct. It may appear once per tuple pattern: `(first, .., last)` is fine, `(.., x, ..)` is ambiguous.

The difference between `_` and `_s` matters when ownership is involved:

blocks.output:
found a string
Some("Hello!")
Can't overwrite an existing customized value
setting is Some(5)
Some numbers: 2, 32
blocks.explain: With `if let Some(_s) = s`, the `String` would be moved into `_s` and the `println!` after it would fail to compile.

blocks.output:
error: `..` can only be used once per tuple pattern
 --> src/main.rs:5:22
  |
5 |         (.., second, ..) => println!("Some numbers: {second}"),
  |          --          ^^ can only be used once per tuple pattern
  |          |
  |          previously used here

blocks.title: Match guards
blocks.md:
A **match guard** is an `if` condition after the pattern: `Some(x) if x % 2 == 0 => ...`. The arm matches only if the pattern matches **and** the condition is true. Guards can use variables from outside, which fixes the shadowing problem above. The compiler does not look inside guards when checking exhaustiveness, so you usually still need a final catch-all.

A guard applies to the **whole** `|` list: `4 | 5 | 6 if y` means `(4 | 5 | 6) if y`, not `4 | 5 | (6 if y)`.

blocks.output:
The number 4 is even
Default case, x = Some(5)
no

blocks.title: @ bindings
blocks.md: `name @ pattern` tests a value against a pattern **and** binds the whole value to `name`. Without it, a range pattern tests but gives you no variable:

blocks.output:
Found an id in range: 5
Found an id in another range
Found some other id: 42

blocks.title: Patterns and references
blocks.md:
Matching on a reference raises the question: should the bound variables be copies, moves, or references? *Programming Rust* explains the tools:

- A **`&` pattern** matches a reference and gives you what it points to: `&(x, y)` against a `&(i32, i32)` binds `i32`s. It only works when the parts can be copied (or are themselves moved out of an owned value).
- **`ref` and `ref mut`** bind by reference instead of by move: `Some(ref name)` borrows the `String` inside an owned `Option<String>` without moving it.
- **Default binding modes**: when you match a reference against a non-reference pattern, Rust automatically binds the variables as references. `match &opt { Some(name) => ... }` gives `name: &String`. This is why most modern code rarely writes `ref`.

blocks.output:
hello, Ferris (6 bytes)
still borrowed: Ferris
opt is still usable: Some("Ferris")
(2, "a!")
3 7

blocks.title: Pattern syntax at a glance
rows: any alternative; all must bind the same names
by field name; `..` skips the rest
matches a reference, gives the target
binds by reference instead of moving
tests and binds the whole value
not part of the pattern; an extra condition on the arm

blocks.title: A tiny command parser
blocks.md: Split each input line into words and match on the **slice** of words. Use slice patterns, literals, `@` with a range and a guard. Commands: `go <dir>` with `dir` one of north/south/east/west; `take <item>`; `drop all`; `wait <n>` where `n` parses and is between 1 and 9; anything else is unknown.
blocks.task: Print `going north`, `taking lamp`, `dropping everything`, `waiting 3 turns`, `unknown: wait 30`, `unknown: dance`.
blocks.expected_output:
going north
taking lamp
dropping everything
waiting 3 turns
unknown: wait 30
unknown: dance
hints: String literals can appear in slice patterns of `&str`: `["take", item] => ...`.

blocks.title: Pattern drills
blocks.goal: Use ranges, |, struct and slice patterns, guards and @ bindings to replace chains of if statements.
blocks.behavior:
Write each function with a single `match` (helpers allowed):
- `pub fn http_class(code: u16) -> &'static str`: 100–199 `"informational"`, 200–299 `"success"`, 300–399 `"redirect"`, 400–499 `"client error"`, 500–599 `"server error"`, anything else `"invalid"`.
- `pub fn quadrant(p: Point) -> String` for `pub struct Point { pub x: i32, pub y: i32 }`: `"origin"`, `"x axis"`, `"y axis"`, or `"Q1"`..`"Q4"` (Q1 is x > 0, y > 0; counter-clockwise).
- `pub fn summarize(v: &[i32]) -> String`: `"empty"`; one item `"just N"`; if the first and last are equal (2+ items) `"bookends N"`; otherwise `"N..M (K items)"` with first, last and length.
- `pub fn ticket(age: u32, student: bool) -> u32` (price in euros): 0–5 → 0; 6–17 → 5; students 18–25 → 6; 65 and over → 7; everyone else 10.
- `pub fn describe(t: Token) -> String` for `pub enum Token { Num(i64), Op(char), Ident(String) }`: small numbers 0–9 → `"digit N"`; other numbers `"number N"`; `+ - * /` → `"operator X"`; any other op char → `"unknown op X"`; an identifier starting with `_` → `"private NAME"`; else `"name NAME"`.
hints: `[first, .., last] if first == last => ...` must come before the general `[first, .., last]` arm.
blocks.solution_explain: Each function is one `match` that reads like the specification. Order matters: the guarded `bookends` arm and the `digit` arm must come before the more general arms that would also match.

blocks.title: Simplifying expressions
blocks.goal: Match deeply nested enums through Box, combining nested patterns, guards and | to rewrite a tree.
blocks.behavior:
Given
```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub enum Expr {
    Num(i64),
    Var(String),
    Add(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    Mul(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    Neg(Box<Expr>),
}
```
write `pub fn simplify(e: Expr) -> Expr` that simplifies the children first (bottom-up), then applies these rules until none applies at the top:
- `Num(a) + Num(b)` → `Num(a + b)`; `Num(a) * Num(b)` → `Num(a * b)`
- `x + 0` and `0 + x` → `x`
- `x * 1` and `1 * x` → `x`
- `x * 0` and `0 * x` → `Num(0)`
- `-(Num(n))` → `Num(-n)`; `-(-x)` → `x`
Also `pub fn eval(e: &Expr, x: i64) -> i64` where every `Var` has the value `x`.
hints: Box patterns are not available in stable Rust. Simplify the children, then match on a **tuple of references**: `match (&a, &b) { (Expr::Num(x), Expr::Num(y)) => ..., (Expr::Num(0), _) => ..., ... }`.
For the `x + 0` cases: `(_, Expr::Num(0)) => a` returns the left child unchanged.
`Expr::Neg(inner)`: simplify `*inner`, then match the result: `Expr::Num(n) => Expr::Num(-n)`, `Expr::Neg(x) => *x`, `other => Expr::Neg(Box::new(other))`.
blocks.solution_explain: Simplifying the children first means every rule only has to look one level deep. Matching on `(&a, &b)` tests the shapes without moving `a` and `b`, so an arm can still return one of them whole. `(_, Expr::Num(0)) | (Expr::Num(0), _)` uses `|` across tuple patterns. `leaf => leaf` passes `Num` and `Var` through unchanged.

questions.q: In `match x { Some(y) => ... }` with an outer variable `y = 10`, what does the inner `y` do?
options: Binds a new variable that shadows the outer y
`4 if y | 5 if y | 6 if y` only for 6
questions.explanation: The guard applies to the whole alternative list.

questions.q: What is the difference between `_` and `_x`?
options: `_x` binds (and can move) the value; `_` does not bind
questions.explanation: That matters for owned values like String.

questions.q: Which pattern binds the tail of a slice?
Fill in the binding operator: `Message::Hello { id: id __ 3..=7 }`
questions.explanation: id @ 3..=7 tests the range and binds the value.

questions.q: `match &opt { Some(name) => ... }` where `opt: Option<String>`. What is the type of name?
questions.explanation: Default binding modes bind by reference.

points: Literals, `|` and ranges (`..=`, `a..`) test values; plain names bind and shadow.
Struct, enum, tuple, array and slice patterns mirror the data and nest freely.
`_` ignores without binding, `_x` binds silently, `..` skips the rest (once per tuple).
Guards add conditions to an arm; `@` tests and binds together.
Matching a reference binds by reference automatically; `&` patterns and `ref` give explicit control.

terms.def: An if condition after a pattern in a match arm that must also be true for the arm to run.
Syntax name @ pattern that tests a value against a pattern and binds it to a name.
A pattern like [first, .., last] that matches slices of varying length.
The rule that matching a reference against a non-reference pattern binds variables by reference.
A pattern keyword that binds by reference instead of moving the value.
